title: Making amends
hookLine: repair where you can, without causing more harm

cards: A borrowed drill comes back with a cracked case. The borrower says sorry, means it, and hands it over. The owner says no problem.
And the drill is still cracked. Words can mend a lot between two people. They can't mend a drill.

Between I'm sorry and the end of the matter there's a second step, older than any apology study: putting back what you can. An old law in the book of Numbers spells it out, down to a fraction. Today: making amends.

teach.h: CONFESS, THEN PUT IT BACK, PLUS A FIFTH.

teach.b: Numbers, chapter five, describes someone who has wronged another person: "Then they shall confess their sin which they have done: and he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof, and give it unto him against whom he hath trespassed."
Confession comes first, but the words don't close the matter. Then the principal, the thing itself, put back, and a fifth on top. Second, where it goes: to the one wronged.
Not a general donation, not a vague promise to be better. The repair has a name and an address. Third, the limit.
Alcoholics Anonymous, in its Big Book, describes making direct amends to the people one has harmed, wherever possible, except when doing so would injure them or others.
Sometimes contacting someone would reopen a wound they've worked hard to close. Repair that causes fresh harm isn't repair. Fourth, when you can't go back.

teach.h: NO ONE TO RECEIVE IT? IT STILL GOES.
teach.b: The next verse in Numbers imagines a wronged man with no kinsman left to receive the repayment, and it still gets paid, to the Lord, through the priest. The debt finds another place to go.

Some people today make what's sometimes called a living amend: changing the behavior for good, or doing for someone else what they owed the person they can't reach. Making it right isn't always making it undone.
It's the most honest repair the situation allows.

how: In Alcoholics Anonymous, members work through making amends to people they've harmed, often with a sponsor's help in deciding when direct contact would cause harm; some readers of Numbers 5 take its pattern, confession first and then repayment to the person wronged, as a model for amends today.

o: saying sorry again, more seriously this time
promising in general to be a better person
putting back what you took or broke, where you can

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.

s: in Numbers 5, confessing settles the matter on its own
after confessing comes repayment: the principal, plus a fifth, to the one wronged.
the Big Book describes amends wherever possible, except when they would injure others
repair that causes fresh harm isn't repair.
in Numbers 5, if the wronged man has no kinsman, the debt is cancelled
it's still paid, to the Lord, through the priest. the debt finds another place to go.

games.q: under the law in Numbers 5, you've wronged a neighbor and confessed it. what comes next?
o: nothing more; the confession was enough.
pay back what you took, add a fifth, and give it to the one you wronged.
give the same amount to anyone in need.
games.why: "he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof, and give it unto him against whom he hath trespassed."

practice: Bring to mind one thing you owe someone, not a feeling but a thing: a borrowed book, a broken promise, a credit you took, a loan, an hour of help.

Ask slowly what would put it back, and whether doing that would hurt them or anyone else. If the road is open, choose one concrete step; if it's closed, picture who could receive a living amend in their place.

wordCard.voice: Making amends. Putting back what you can, specifically, without causing fresh harm along the way. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: make it right. Sorry is the words; amends are the thing put back. That's day nine hundred seventy-nine.
